source("../_common.R")

Chapter 3 of [Black Hat Bash](https://nostarch.com/blackhatbash) (by Dolev Farhi and Nick Aleks) builds a hacking lab on a local virtual machine. I didn't want that lab on my laptop. A machine full of deliberately vulnerable services is the kind of thing I'd rather keep somewhere I can stop, snapshot, and throw away. In this post I'll cover how I moved the book's lab onto an AWS EC2 instance, and how each of the book's safety precautions translates to the cloud.

## What does the lab need?

The book's lab is one Kali Linux machine. Kali plays both roles: it hosts the targets, and it's the machine we attack them from. The book's minimum specifications are 4 GB of RAM, 40 GB of storage, and an internet connection for the install.

The targets are eight Docker containers that belong to a fictional hosting company, ACME Infinity Servers. They're split across two Docker networks:

* Public network (`172.16.10.0/24`): the entry points, with names that start with `p-`.
* Corporate network (`10.1.0.0/24`): the backend machines, with names that start with `c-`.

Both networks are Docker bridges, and a Docker bridge is just a virtual network switch that lives inside one machine. I've found this is the detail that makes the move to AWS simple. The targets never get an address in AWS, so the cloud only has to provide the Kali machine.

The diagram below shows the layout. My laptop reaches the Kali instance over SSH, and the Kali instance reaches the containers through its two bridges:

The security group lets in SSH from one address and blocks everything else. Inside the instance, `p-web-02` and `c-jumpbox-01` sit on both bridges. Later chapters use them to pivot from the public network into the corporate one.

## What changes from the book?

The book gives three precautions for any hacking lab. Each one has an AWS counterpart:

| Book precaution | On AWS |
|:---|:---|
| Keep the lab off the internet | The security group allows SSH from my IP address only, and the targets live on bridges that never leave the instance |
| Separate the lab from your main operating system | The lab runs on its own instance in its own VPC |
| Take frequent snapshots | Save an AMI whenever the lab is in a good state |

The first row changes the most. A cloud instance is on the internet by definition, so we can't work offline the way the book suggests. Instead, we make sure nothing outside the instance can reach the lab, and only SSH from one address can reach the instance.

```{r}
#| label: co_box_aup
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "r",
  header = "Only attack what you own",
  contents = "AWS lets you run security tests against your own resources, and only your own. Every target in this lab is a container on the Kali instance. Never point these tools at an address, host, or service you don't own or don't have written permission to test.")
```

## Setting up the network

You don't have to know much about AWS for this, but you'll need an account and the [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/) configured with credentials. Each command below has a console equivalent if you'd rather click through it.

### Creating a VPC

A VPC (virtual private cloud) is a private network inside your AWS account. A dedicated VPC keeps the lab away from anything else in the account. The command below creates one:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.50.0.0/16 \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=lab-vpc}]'
```

The VPC range (`10.50.0.0/16`) was chosen so it doesn't overlap either lab network. That way the Docker bridges and the VPC never compete for the same addresses.

The VPC also needs one public subnet with a route to an internet gateway, or we can't SSH in. The console handles this in one step: choose VPC, then Create VPC, then VPC and more, with one availability zone, one public subnet, no private subnets, and no NAT gateway.

### Creating a security group

A security group is the instance's firewall. Ours allows exactly one thing: SSH from my current public IP address. The commands below create the group and add that rule:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
VPC_ID=vpc-xxxxxxxx

aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name lab-kali-sg \
  --description "Kali lab" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID"

MY_IP=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com)

aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xxxxxxxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 22 \
  --cidr "${MY_IP}/32"
```

There are no other inbound rules. If my home IP address changes, SSH stops working until I update the rule with the new address.

### Creating a key pair

The Kali instance accepts SSH keys, not passwords. The commands below create a key, save it to `~/.ssh/`, and make it readable by my user only (SSH refuses a key file other users can read):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name lab-key \
  --query 'KeyMaterial' --output text > ~/.ssh/lab-key.pem
chmod 400 ~/.ssh/lab-key.pem
```

## Launching Kali

OffSec publishes an official Kali image on the [AWS Marketplace](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace). Search for "Kali Linux", subscribe to the listing once in the console, and copy the AMI ID for your region from its launch page.

The default root volume is too small for the book's 40 GB minimum, so we set the size at launch. The root device name varies between images, and I look it up rather than guess:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 describe-images --image-ids ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
  --query 'Images[0].RootDeviceName' --output text
```

Now we can launch the instance. Replace `/dev/xvda` below with the name `describe-images` returned. A `t3.large` (2 vCPUs, 8 GB of RAM) doubles the book's memory minimum, and that headroom helps once eight containers are running:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
  --instance-type t3.large \
  --key-name lab-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-xxxxxxxx \
  --subnet-id subnet-xxxxxxxx \
  --associate-public-ip-address \
  --block-device-mappings '[{"DeviceName":"/dev/xvda","Ebs":{"VolumeSize":60}}]' \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=kali-lab}]'
```

The login user on the Kali image is `kali`. We can confirm the instance is reachable by connecting with the key:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
ssh -i ~/.ssh/lab-key.pem kali@<public-ip>
```

## Preparing Kali

The book's preparation steps carry over unchanged. First we update the packages:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo apt update -y
sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt dist-upgrade -y
```

Newer Kali releases use `zsh` as the default shell, but the book's scripts assume bash. The command below makes bash the default for the `kali` user:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo usermod --shell /bin/bash kali
```

The change takes effect at the next login, so I disconnect and connect again over SSH. We can confirm the new shell with `echo $SHELL`, which should print `/bin/bash`.

## Deploying the lab

The book walks through installing Docker and each tool by hand, and I'd recommend doing that once to see what gets installed. On a fresh instance, though, the repository's `make init` does all of it. The commands below clone the repository and run it:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/dolevf/Black-Hat-Bash.git
cd Black-Hat-Bash/lab
sudo make init
```

The first run downloads every image and tool, so expect it to take a while. A second SSH session can follow the install log:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
tail -f /var/log/lab-install.log
```

### Checking the lab

When the log says the install has finished, `make test` checks that the lab is running:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo make test
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
Lab is up.
```

:::

Next, `docker ps` should list all eight containers (the order may differ):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo docker ps --format "{{.Names}}"
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
p-web-01
p-web-02
p-ftp-01
c-jumpbox-01
c-db-01
c-db-02
c-backup-01
c-redis-01
```

:::

Last, the two bridge interfaces should carry the gateway addresses from the book (`172.16.10.1` and `10.1.0.1`):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
ip addr | grep "br_"
```

These addresses exist only on the Kali instance. From my laptop, an address like `172.16.10.10` goes nowhere, and that's exactly the isolation we want.

## Running a lab session

Once the lab is built, every session follows the same loop. The diagram below shows it:

```{mermaid}
%%| eval: true
%%| fig-align: 'center'
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'darkMode':false}}}%%

flowchart TD
    Start(["Start<br>instance"]) --> IP("Look up the<br>public IP")
    IP --> SSH("ssh in")
    SSH --> Deploy("make deploy")
    Deploy --> Work("Work through<br>the chapter")
    Work --> Good{"Lab in a<br>good state?"}
    Good -->|"yes"| AMI[("Save<br>an AMI")]
    Good -->|"no"| Down("make teardown")
    AMI --> Down
    Down --> Stop(["Stop<br>instance"])

    style Start fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333
    style Stop fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333
    style IP fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style SSH fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style Deploy fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style Work fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style Good fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF
    style AMI fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF
    style Down fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
```

The book's lab commands (`make deploy` and `make teardown`) work the same on EC2. AWS adds the steps at each end: starting and stopping the instance, and saving an AMI.

### Starting and connecting

A stopped instance gets a new public IP address each time it starts. The commands below start the instance and print the new address:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].PublicIpAddress' --output text
```

An Elastic IP would keep the address fixed, but it costs money while the instance is stopped. For a lab I use a few times a week, looking up the address is cheaper.

### Saving an AMI

The book recommends a snapshot whenever the lab is in a good state. On AWS, an AMI (Amazon Machine Image) captures the whole instance, and we can launch a fresh copy from it if the lab breaks:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 create-image --instance-id i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
  --name kali-lab-clean --description "Black Hat Bash lab after make init"
```

AWS reboots the instance while it creates the image, unless we pass `--no-reboot`. I let it reboot, because the reboot writes everything to disk before AWS copies it.

### Stopping the instance

EC2 bills for the instance while it runs. When I'm done for the day, I tear down the lab and then stop (not terminate) the instance:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo make teardown
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

A stopped instance keeps its volume, so everything we installed is there next time. The volume still costs a little while the instance is stopped.

## Throw it away?

Stopping the instance is the right default between sessions, but it isn't free and it isn't clean. I've found three reasons to terminate the lab instead.

The first reason is cost. A stopped instance no longer bills for compute, but its 60 GB volume bills every month whether I use it or not. An AMI is cheaper to keep, because its snapshot stores only the blocks in use. If I won't be back for a few weeks, the AMI is the only copy I need.

The second reason is a clean slate. Each chapter compromises the containers, and the work leaves files, credentials, and changed configurations behind on Kali. The book's advice to take snapshots exists for this: a lab should return to a known state. Launching a new instance from the AMI gets me that state with certainty, without having to remember what I changed.

The third reason is drift. Kali is a rolling release, so an instance left stopped for months needs a long upgrade before it's useful. When the break is that long, a fresh image from the Marketplace and a new `make init` are often faster than upgrading the old one.

The diagram below shows how I decide at the end of a session:

```{mermaid}
%%| eval: true
%%| fig-align: 'center'
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'darkMode':false}}}%%

flowchart TD
    Done(["Session<br>done"]) --> Soon{"Back within<br>a week?"}
    Soon -->|"yes"| Stop("Stop the<br>instance")
    Soon -->|"no"| Keep{"Lab worth<br>keeping?"}
    Keep -->|"yes"| AMI[("Save<br>an AMI")]
    Keep -->|"no"| Term("Terminate the<br>instance")
    AMI --> Term
    Term --> Gone(["Nothing left<br>running"])

    style Done fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333
    style Gone fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333
    style Soon fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF
    style Keep fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF
    style Stop fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
    style AMI fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF
    style Term fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5
```

Before terminating, make sure the AMI exists and is ready. The command below prints its state, which should be `available`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 describe-images --owners self \
  --filters "Name=name,Values=kali-lab-clean" \
  --query 'Images[0].[ImageId,State]' --output text
```

```{r}
#| label: co_box_terminate
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "r",
  header = "Terminating is permanent",
  contents = "Terminating an instance deletes its root volume. Unless you've saved an AMI first, every tool, image, and change to the lab goes with it.")
```

Once the AMI is `available`, we can terminate the instance:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

The next session starts with `run-instances`, using the AMI ID in place of the Marketplace image. The VPC, security group, and key pair stay in place, and none of them cost anything while they sit unused.

When I'm finished with the book, the AMI goes too. Deregistering an AMI doesn't delete its snapshot, so that takes a second command:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 deregister-image --image-id ami-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
aws ec2 delete-snapshot --snapshot-id snap-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

## Recap

The Black Hat Bash lab moves to EC2 without changes to the lab itself, because every target is a container on the Kali instance. AWS replaces the hypervisor, the security group replaces the book's advice to stay offline, and AMIs replace VM snapshots. Stopping the instance between sessions keeps the bill down without losing any work.
